entry.title: My agentic coding workflow
entry.summary: How I build with AI agents every day: Claude writes the code, I write the rules once and make the decisions.
entry.content:
I build with AI agents every day, and my agentic coding workflow is pretty simple. I write down what I want and how things should be done, Claude does the work, and I make the decisions.

When I redesigned this site, it took two days. Claude wrote all the code, including a small game called Shiba Land. I reviewed what it made and said what to keep.

One project per product

Each of my products has its own Claude Project: this site, Rillow, Bundle and Unposed. I tell the project what I need, and it starts a separate thread for each task, so several things get done at the same time. I just check what's finished and what needs me, on my laptop or my phone.

Boris Cherny, who made Claude Code, used to juggle ten or more sessions by hand (VentureBeat). A project does that for me. I wrote more about it in how I use Claude Projects.

I write the rules down once

Every project has a short paragraph of instructions, and the code has an AGENTS.md file that explains how the site is built and what the design rules are. Most of those rules are there because I said no to something once, like "never use green". When I correct Claude, I tell it to remember, so I never have to say it twice.

Mitchell Hashimoto calls this engineering the harness: when an agent makes a mistake, you fix its instructions so it doesn't happen again (My AI Adoption Journey).

Claude writes the code, I make the calls

Agents are great at building things. What they can't do is tell which version feels right. Most of my replies are a couple of words, like "too colourful", "i love it" or "Pixel is better".

That's most of my job now. Simon Willison says writing code is cheap now, and when trying three versions takes a few minutes, picking the right one is the work.

My setup

Claude can only use what it can reach, so I connect my tools: GitHub for code, Rillow (my SEO product) for keyword research and briefs, and my Mac through Remote Control for things that only run there, like the design app Paper and the iOS simulator.

This post was made the same way. Claude researched the topic, got a brief from Rillow and wrote a draft. I told it the draft sounded like a computer wrote it, so we rewrote it.

What I keep for myself

I decide what to build, and I approve anything that can't be undone. On this site every push goes live, so I always see a preview first. Anything with my name on it, I check myself.

What still goes wrong

Instructions can be wrong. My first project setup got the branch wrong, and Claude caught it by reading the code. It's also bad at drawing from scratch: the first Shiba drawings came out silly. It works much better with clear rules, like pixel art, or with a design I've already made. And long threads get slow and expensive, so I start a new thread for new work.

If you want to try this

Pick one side project and make it a Claude Project. Write a short paragraph on where the code is, how to check changes and what needs your OK. Ask for a preview before anything ships, keep your answers short, and when you correct Claude, tell it to remember.

If you're hiring for this kind of work, my CV has the rest.

entry.title: How to use Claude Projects the right way
entry.summary: How to set up and use the new Claude Projects: instructions, memory, threads and keeping usage down, with examples from my own site.
entry.content:
If you want to know how to use Claude Projects well, think of a project as one ongoing piece of work. You set it up once and then keep sending it tasks. I run this site, davit.cc, in a project, so the examples here are from my own setup.

What a project is now

Anthropic redesigned Projects in September 2026. A project used to be a folder of files and chats. Now it's a chat with a coordinator that starts a separate thread for each task, and each thread is a full Claude Code session with its own copy of your code. Threads share a memory and report back when they're done.

Projects are in beta on the Pro and Max plans and work in the web, desktop and mobile apps (docs). A lot of guides online still describe the old version.

When to make one

Make a project when the work keeps going: a product, a website, a long migration. For a single task, a normal session is enough. My site is the ongoing kind. The redesign, a new favicon, a few small experiments and this blog all happened in the same project.

Let Claude set it up

I didn't write my setup myself. My first message in the new project was:

Help me set up this new project from my recent work. Look through my recent sessions and repositories, identify the main thread of work, and propose a project setup: a short name, the repositories it should include, an environment, concise project instructions drawn from what kept coming up, and one or two optional routines. Show me the proposal before changing anything.

Claude came back with a name, instructions and a weekly check of the live site, and I said yes.

Keep the instructions short

Project instructions are the rules every thread reads first. Keep them short: where the code is, how to check changes and what needs your OK. Mine are one paragraph:

Site is davit.cc, built from the main branch of davit-khaburdzania.github.io and served by a Cloudflare Worker (wrangler.jsonc). Davit is the only one working on the site, so don't open pull requests: commit and push straight to main. Every push to main deploys davit.cc automatically within about a minute (Cloudflare's GitHub connection), so a push is a production change: show Davit a preview of visual changes before pushing. Keep profile details (location "Tbilisi, Georgia", website davit.cc) consistent across the site, GitHub and LinkedIn. Verify changes on the live site after each push.

The first version got the branch wrong, and the first thread fixed it after reading the code. Rules get added as you go. "No pull requests" came a day later, when I said I'm the only one working on the site.

Instructions, memory and CLAUDE.md

A project keeps context in three places:

Where What goes in it Example from davit.cc
Project instructions Rules every thread needs from the start Push straight to main, and show a preview first
Project memory Decisions Claude picks up as you work The favicon uses the pixel-art Shiba
CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md in the repo How the code is built and styled "Never use green accents."

Memory fills up when you ask, like "remember that Unposed goes last in the Projects list". If you only write one of the three, make it the file in your repo, because every session reads it, in a project or not.

Send work and walk away

Talk to the coordinator like a colleague. Questions get answered right away, and new work becomes a thread. When a thread needs a decision, it asks with a few options and a recommendation, and you pick one. You can also tell it how you like to work, like "ask before starting new threads".

One thing isn't obvious: when a thread needs your approval, you answer inside that thread. Saying "go ahead" to the coordinator doesn't reach it.

Run work on your own computer

Some work needs your own machine. For me that's Paper, a design app that only runs on my Mac. A project can run that one thread on your computer through Remote Control while the rest stays in the cloud. Turn it on in the desktop app under Settings > Claude Code, then pick "Work locally" in the project chat.

Keep usage under control

Projects use your plan faster than a single chat, because every thread is a full session and several can run at once. You can switch to cheaper models in the project settings. Long threads get expensive too, so start a fresh thread for new work and close the ones you're done with.

Frequently asked questions

When should I use a project instead of a chat?

When the work keeps going, like a product or a site you keep improving. A quick question is fine in a chat.

What's the difference between Claude Projects and Claude Code?

Projects are built on Claude Code. Every thread is a Claude Code session, and the project adds the coordinator, shared instructions and memory.

Can I share a Claude Project with my team?

Not yet. During the beta a project belongs to one person.

Do cloud threads get my local skills and MCP servers?

No. Cloud threads get the connectors and skills from your claude.ai account and whatever is in your repo. Anything installed only on your laptop needs a thread running on your computer.

I wrote more about how I work day to day in my agentic coding workflow, and my CV has the rest.

entry.title: Languages and frameworks don't matter anymore
entry.summary: With AI agents writing most of the code, the stack matters much less than it used to. Why I think so, and what still matters.
entry.content:
Picking the stack used to be the first big decision on any project. Now that AI agents write most of the code, I don't think it matters much. If you're asking what the best language for AI coding is, my answer is any language where the agent can quickly check its own work, that has plenty of public code to learn from, and that you can still read.

I've used a lot of stacks

In 15+ years I've worked with Ruby on Rails, Elixir, Node.js, TypeScript, Python and React, and the stack changed with almost every job (my Experience section has the full list). Back then it mattered a lot. The stack decided who you could hire and how fast you could move.

What changed

Agents now write most of the code, in whatever language you use. Andrej Karpathy says agents write almost all of his code now (Yahoo Tech), and Simon Willison puts it simply: writing code is cheap now.

This year I've built a Next.js app for Rillow, an iPhone app, an Android app and a Chrome extension for Bundle, and this site in plain HTML. Each time the platform picked the language, and Claude handled all of them.

Languages still differ a bit

There is some evidence that languages aren't equal for agents. José Valim, who created Elixir, points to a benchmark where Elixir scored highest (Why Elixir is the best language for AI). GitHub points to a study where almost all compile errors in AI-written code were type errors, which typed languages like TypeScript catch early (GitHub blog). Armin Ronacher, who wrote Flask, likes Go and TypeScript for agents (A Language for Agents).

Look at why, though. Every one of those reasons comes back to fast feedback: a compiler or tests that tell the agent right away when something is wrong. That comes from the tooling much more than from the language.

What still matters

The big one is whether the agent can check its own work. Fast tests and a strict type checker do more than switching languages. Clear conventions help too, because a codebase with one way of doing things is easier for agents and for people. The platform still matters, since an iPhone app goes through Xcode and App Review whatever you write it in. And you still own what ships, so pick something you can read.

So what's the best language for AI coding?

For a new web app I'd pick TypeScript with strict checks. If your team already knows Rails or Elixir, stay with it and write good tests. Agents can work in any of them. What they can't handle is a codebase with no way to check their work.

What this means for hiring

Years in one framework matter less now. I'd look for people who can split work into small tasks, check the results properly and decide what not to build.

When I still choose carefully

Code where performance is the product, native platform work and very new languages with little public code still deserve a careful choice. For everything else, pick what fits the platform, keep the feedback fast and spend the time you save on the product.

If you want to see how I work day to day, read my agentic coding workflow. My CV has the rest.
